title: The ECG
summary: Read an electrocardiogram systematically, from rate to ischemia.

lessons.title: Waves, Intervals and the Conduction System

levels.kid:
Your heart has its own tiny electric wires. Every heartbeat starts with a little spark in a spot at the top of the heart called the SA node. It is like the heart's drummer.

The spark spreads over the top rooms first, then waits a tiny moment at a gate, then zooms down to the big bottom rooms so they squeeze hard.

An ECG is a machine with sticky stickers on your skin. It listens to that electricity and draws it as wiggly lines. The small bump is the top rooms. The big spike is the bottom rooms squeezing. The gentle hill after is the heart resetting. Doctors read those wiggles like a secret message!
levels.hs:
An electrocardiogram (ECG or EKG) records the heart's electrical activity from electrodes on the skin. Each heartbeat makes a repeating pattern:
- **P wave**: the atria (upper chambers) depolarize, meaning their cells fire electrically. This triggers atrial contraction.
- **PR interval**: from the start of P to the start of QRS. It includes the pause at the AV node, which gives the atria time to finish filling the ventricles. Normal is 0.12 to 0.20 seconds.
- **QRS complex**: the ventricles depolarize. It is tall because the ventricles have much more muscle. Normal is narrower than 0.12 seconds.
- **T wave**: the ventricles repolarize (reset).
- **QT interval**: start of QRS to end of T, the whole ventricular electrical cycle.

The signal's path is the conduction system: SA node (the natural pacemaker) → atria → AV node (the delay) → bundle of His → left and right bundle branches → Purkinje fibers spreading through the ventricles.

ECG paper runs at a standard speed. One small box is 0.04 seconds and one big box (5 small boxes) is 0.20 seconds. That is how you measure intervals with a ruler instead of a stopwatch.
levels.college:
The ECG records the summed electrical vectors of the myocardium as projected onto each lead. Depolarization moving toward a positive electrode produces an upward deflection; moving away produces a downward one.

Conduction sequence and its ECG correlates:
- **SA node** fires spontaneously (phase 4 depolarization via the funny current) and sets sinus rhythm. Its firing is invisible on the surface ECG.
- **Atrial depolarization** = P wave. Atrial repolarization is buried in the QRS.
- **AV node** conducts slowly (calcium-channel dependent tissue), producing most of the PR interval. This delay protects the ventricles from very fast atrial rates.
- **His-Purkinje system** conducts rapidly, so normal ventricular activation is quick and synchronous: a narrow QRS.
- **Ventricular repolarization** = ST segment and T wave.

Normal values to memorize:
- PR 120 to 200 ms. Long = AV conduction delay (first-degree block). Short = a pathway bypassing the AV node (pre-excitation) or a junctional focus.
- QRS under 120 ms. Wide = a bundle branch block, ventricular origin, pre-excitation, hyperkalemia or drug effect.
- QTc (QT corrected for heart rate) roughly under 440 to 460 ms, slightly higher in women. QT shortens as heart rate rises, so it must be corrected (Bazett formula: QT divided by the square root of the RR interval).

Standard calibration: paper at 25 mm/s, so 1 mm = 0.04 s and 5 mm = 0.20 s; amplitude 10 mm = 1 mV.

The 12-lead ECG combines 6 limb leads (I, II, III, aVR, aVL, aVF; the frontal plane) and 6 precordial leads (V1 to V6; the horizontal plane). Each lead is a different camera angle on the same electrical event, which is why an infarct in one wall shows up only in the leads looking at it.
levels.phd:
The surface ECG is a far-field recording: each lead measures the potential difference between electrodes, reflecting the vector sum of millions of cellular dipoles. The cellular basis lies in the ventricular action potential. Phase 0 is the rapid sodium influx; phase 1 an early repolarizing notch from transient outward potassium current; phase 2 the plateau balanced by L-type calcium influx and delayed rectifier potassium efflux; phase 3 repolarization driven by IKr (hERG channel) and IKs; phase 4 rest maintained by IK1.

The QRS reflects the wavefront of phase 0 sweeping through the ventricles, roughly endocardium to epicardium. The T wave reflects dispersion of repolarization. Because epicardial cells have shorter action potentials than endocardial and midmyocardial (M) cells, the epicardium repolarizes first, so the repolarization vector points the same way as depolarization. That is why the normal T wave is upright in leads where the QRS is upright, despite being the electrically opposite process.

The QT interval is a proxy for ventricular action-potential duration. Block of IKr by many drugs, or congenital channelopathies (long QT types 1 to 3 involving KCNQ1, KCNH2 and SCN5A), prolong phase 3, increase dispersion of repolarization and permit early afterdepolarizations, the substrate for torsades de pointes. Heart-rate correction is imperfect: Bazett overcorrects at high rates, so Fridericia (cube root of RR) is preferred in drug trials.

The AV node has decremental conduction: the faster it is stimulated, the slower it conducts. This property filters atrial fibrillation and flutter. Dual AV-nodal pathways (fast and slow) underlie AV nodal reentrant tachycardia.

Einthoven's triangle formalizes the limb leads (lead II = lead I + lead III), and Wilson's central terminal provides the reference for the unipolar precordial leads, which is why the 12 leads are mathematically redundant yet clinically indispensable.
levels.expert:
Clinicians read ECGs with a fixed sequence so nothing is skipped: rate, rhythm, axis, intervals (PR, QRS, QT), then morphology (P waves, QRS, ST segments, T waves), and finally comparison with an old ECG. The comparison step catches more pathology than any single criterion.

Practical pitfalls in the basics:
- **Lead reversal**. The most common is swapping the left and right arm electrodes: lead I becomes inverted (negative P, QRS and T in I) and aVR looks upright. Before calling dextrocardia or a lateral infarct, suspect the technician. True dextrocardia also shows loss of R-wave progression across V1 to V6.
- **Calibration**. Check the calibration mark. Half-standard recordings (5 mm = 1 mV) are used when voltages are huge and will make you underestimate hypertrophy or ST deviation.
- **QT measurement**. Measure in the lead with the longest QT (often II or V5) and use the tangent method for the end of the T wave; do not include a separate U wave. Machine QTc readings are unreliable with wide QRS, atrial fibrillation or flat T waves. In a wide QRS, part of the QT is depolarization, so the JT interval is sometimes used instead.
- **PR segment**. Depression of the PR segment, with diffuse ST elevation, suggests pericarditis; elevation of PR in aVR is the mirror image.

Clinical anchors: a short PR with a slurred upstroke of the QRS (delta wave) is Wolff-Parkinson-White pre-excitation, important because AV-nodal blockers given during pre-excited atrial fibrillation can accelerate conduction down the accessory pathway. A long QT with syncope, especially triggered by exertion, emotion or loud noise, demands review of drugs and electrolytes (potassium, magnesium, calcium) and evaluation for a congenital channelopathy.

And always read the patient alongside the paper. An ECG answers a clinical question; it rarely replaces one.

keyPoints: P = atrial depolarization; QRS = ventricular depolarization; T = ventricular repolarization
Conduction: SA node → atria → AV node (delay) → His bundle → bundle branches → Purkinje fibers
Normal PR 120-200 ms; QRS under 120 ms; QTc roughly under 440-460 ms
At 25 mm/s, 1 small box = 0.04 s and 1 large box = 0.20 s
12 leads = 6 limb (frontal plane) + 6 precordial (horizontal plane) views of the same heartbeat

test.q: Which part of the ECG represents atrial depolarization?
test.explain: The P wave is atrial depolarization. QRS is ventricular depolarization and T is ventricular repolarization.

test.q: Where does the normal heartbeat start?
test.explain: The sinoatrial (SA) node in the right atrium is the natural pacemaker. The AV node is the delay station, not the starting point.

test.q: The PR interval mainly reflects:
choices: Conduction delay through the AV node
test.explain: Most of the PR interval is the slow conduction through the AV node, which lets the atria finish filling the ventricles.

test.q: A QRS duration of 150 ms is best described as:
test.explain: Normal QRS is under 120 ms. 150 ms is wide, suggesting a bundle branch block, ventricular origin, pre-excitation, hyperkalemia or drug effect.

test.q: Why is the QRS complex taller than the P wave?
choices: The ventricles have much more muscle mass
The AV node amplifies the signal
The P wave is filtered by the machine
test.explain: Amplitude reflects the mass of tissue depolarizing. The ventricles are far more muscular than the thin-walled atria.

test.q: Why can't you see atrial repolarization on a normal ECG?
choices: It appears as the U wave
It is buried inside the QRS complex
It happens before the P wave
test.explain: Atrial repolarization occurs at the same time as the much larger ventricular depolarization, so it is hidden in the QRS.

test.q: What does a PR interval of 240 ms with every P followed by a QRS suggest?
test.explain: PR over 200 ms with 1:1 conduction is first-degree AV block, a conduction delay rather than a true block of beats.

test.q: Why must the QT interval be corrected for heart rate?
choices: QT shortens as heart rate rises
QT gets longer as the heart beats faster
QT does not change with heart rate
test.explain: QT naturally shortens at faster rates, so a raw QT can look normal at a fast rate even when it is pathologically long. QTc adjusts for this.

test.q: Which group are the precordial leads?
test.explain: V1 to V6 are the chest (precordial) leads, viewing the heart in the horizontal plane. I, II, III, aVR, aVL and aVF are limb leads.

test.q: At standard speed (25 mm/s), one small box equals ___ seconds.
test.explain: 1 mm at 25 mm/s = 1/25 s = 0.04 s. A large box (5 mm) is 0.20 s.

test.q: The ___ wave represents ventricular repolarization.
test.explain: The T wave is ventricular repolarization. Its direction normally follows the QRS in most leads.

test.q: Name the conduction structure between the AV node and the bundle branches.
test.explain: The bundle of His carries the impulse from the AV node into the septum, where it divides into the left and right bundle branches.

test.q: What is the upper limit of a normal PR interval, in milliseconds?
test.explain: Normal PR is 120 to 200 ms (3 to 5 small boxes).

kidTest.q: What does an ECG draw?
kidTest.explain: An ECG listens to the heart's electricity and draws it as wiggly lines.

kidTest.q: Where does each heartbeat's spark start?
choices: In the SA node, the heart's drummer
kidTest.explain: The SA node at the top of the heart starts every beat, like a drummer keeping time.

kidTest.q: Which rooms of the heart squeeze hardest and make the big spike?
kidTest.explain: The bottom rooms (ventricles) are big and strong, so they make the big spike.

kidTest.q: The small bump before the big spike is from:
kidTest.explain: The little P wave bump is the top rooms (atria) getting their spark.

kidTest.q: What is the gentle hill after the big spike?
kidTest.explain: The T wave is the heart's bottom rooms resetting, ready for the next beat.

kidTest.q: What is the name of the machine that draws the heart's electric wiggles? (3 letters)
kidTest.explain: ECG stands for electrocardiogram. Some people say EKG; it is the same thing.

advancedTest.q: Why is the normal T wave upright in leads where the QRS is upright, even though repolarization is the opposite process of depolarization?
choices: The ECG machine inverts the T wave
Repolarization starts at the endocardium like depolarization
The T wave is generated by the atria
Epicardial cells repolarize first because their action potentials are shorter, so the repolarization wave travels opposite to depolarization
advancedTest.explain: Depolarization runs endocardium → epicardium; repolarization runs epicardium → endocardium. An opposite-polarity process moving in the opposite direction produces a deflection of the same sign.

advancedTest.q: A drug blocks the hERG (IKr) potassium channel. Which ECG change and risk follow?
choices: QT prolongation and risk of torsades de pointes
Peaked P waves and atrial flutter
advancedTest.explain: IKr drives phase 3 repolarization. Blocking it prolongs action potential duration (long QT), allowing early afterdepolarizations that can trigger torsades.

advancedTest.q: Lead I shows negative P, QRS and T waves, aVR is upright, and V1 to V6 show normal R-wave progression. Most likely explanation?
choices: Left and right arm electrodes were swapped
advancedTest.explain: Arm-lead reversal inverts lead I but leaves the precordial leads normal. True dextrocardia also shows loss of R-wave progression across V1 to V6.

advancedTest.q: Which QT correction formula, using the cube root of the RR interval, is preferred over Bazett at high heart rates?
advancedTest.explain: Bazett (square root) overcorrects at fast rates; Fridericia (cube root) is more stable and widely used in drug safety studies.

lessons.title: Rate, Rhythm and Axis

levels.kid:
When doctors look at an ECG, they ask three easy questions first.

One: how fast? They count the big spikes, like counting footsteps. Too fast or too slow can be a problem.

Two: is it steady? A healthy heart goes boom, boom, boom, evenly, like a ticking clock. If the beats are jumbled up, like popcorn popping, something may be wrong.

Three: which way is the electricity going? Normally the spark travels down and to the left, like a slide at the playground. If it slides the wrong way, doctors get curious and look closer.
levels.hs:
Every ECG read starts with rate, rhythm and axis.

**Rate.** Normal adult resting heart rate is 60 to 100 beats per minute. Below 60 is bradycardia; above 100 is tachycardia. Two quick ways to measure:
- **300 rule**: count the big boxes between two R waves and divide 300 by that number. 1 box = 300, 2 = 150, 3 = 100, 4 = 75, 5 = 60, 6 = 50.
- **6-second method**: count the QRS complexes in a 6-second strip and multiply by 10. This works best when the rhythm is irregular.

**Rhythm.** Normal sinus rhythm means: a P wave before every QRS, a QRS after every P wave, the P waves upright in lead II, a regular rhythm, and a rate of 60 to 100. Check if the R-to-R spacing is regular, regularly irregular (a repeating pattern), or irregularly irregular (no pattern at all, typical of atrial fibrillation).

**Axis.** The axis is the average direction of electrical flow through the ventricles. Normally it points down and to the left. A quick check uses two leads:
- Lead I positive and aVF positive = normal axis.
- Lead I positive, aVF negative = possible left axis deviation.
- Lead I negative, aVF positive = right axis deviation.
levels.college:
**Rate.** The 300 method (300 divided by the number of large boxes per R-R interval) or the more precise 1500 method (1500 divided by small boxes) works for regular rhythms. For irregular rhythms, count QRS complexes on a 10-second 12-lead strip and multiply by 6.

**Rhythm.** Define the rhythm by asking: Are there P waves? Is each P followed by a QRS and each QRS preceded by a P? Is the PR constant? Is the QRS narrow (supraventricular origin) or wide (ventricular origin or aberrant conduction)? Is the R-R interval regular? Sinus P waves are upright in I and II and inverted in aVR. Sinus arrhythmia, where the rate speeds with inspiration and slows with expiration, is a normal finding in young people.

**Axis.** The normal QRS axis is −30° to +90°. Left axis deviation (LAD) is beyond −30°; right axis deviation (RAD) is beyond +90°; extreme axis is −90° to ±180°.

The three-lead method:
- I positive, aVF positive: normal.
- I positive, aVF negative: look at lead II. If II is positive, the axis lies between 0° and −30° and is still normal. If II is negative, the axis is beyond −30°: LAD.
- I negative, aVF positive: RAD.
- I negative, aVF negative: extreme axis, suggesting ventricular rhythm or lead error.

Causes of LAD: left anterior fascicular block, inferior myocardial infarction, left ventricular hypertrophy (sometimes), and ventricular pacing. Causes of RAD: right ventricular hypertrophy or strain (for example pulmonary embolism, pulmonary hypertension), left posterior fascicular block, lateral infarction, and normal variation in children and tall thin adults.

Refine the angle by finding the most isoelectric limb lead (equally positive and negative); the axis lies perpendicular to it.
levels.phd:
The mean electrical axis is the frontal-plane projection of the time-integrated QRS vector. The hexaxial reference system arranges the six limb leads at 30° intervals: I at 0°, II at +60°, III at +120°, aVF at +90°, aVL at −30° and aVR at −150°. Each lead records the projection of the instantaneous cardiac vector onto its axis, so the net area of the QRS in each lead is proportional to the cosine of the angle between the mean vector and that lead.

Axis is determined by the anatomy and the conduction system together. The left bundle splits into an anterior and a posterior fascicle. Block of the thin, single-blood-supply left anterior fascicle delays activation of the anterosuperior left ventricle, so late forces point up and left, producing left axis deviation (typically beyond −45°) with qR in I and aVL and rS in II, III and aVF. Left posterior fascicular block is rarer (the posterior fascicle is broad with dual blood supply) and is a diagnosis of exclusion once right ventricular hypertrophy is ruled out.

Rhythm analysis is fundamentally about timing relationships among atrial and ventricular events. Heart rate variability reflects autonomic modulation of the SA node: vagal tone acting via acetylcholine on muscarinic receptors and the IKACh current, and sympathetic tone acting via beta-1 receptors increasing the funny current. Respiratory sinus arrhythmia reflects baroreflex and central respiratory coupling, and reduced variability predicts adverse outcomes after myocardial infarction and in autonomic neuropathy.

The frontal axis is age-dependent. Neonates have right-axis dominance because the right ventricle carried the systemic circulation in utero; the axis shifts leftward through childhood and further with age. Axis interpretation must therefore be calibrated to the patient, and a new shift relative to a prior tracing is more informative than an isolated value.
levels.expert:
Rate, rhythm and axis are the first 20 seconds of every ECG read, and each has traps.

**Rate.** A heart rate of 150 with a narrow regular QRS should make you search for flutter waves: atrial flutter with 2:1 block is the classic missed diagnosis, because every other flutter wave hides in the QRS or T wave. Inverted sawtooth waves in II, III and aVF, or discrete atrial activity in V1, give it away.

**Rhythm.** Ask whether P waves and QRS complexes are married or divorced. AV dissociation (P waves marching through at their own rate unrelated to the QRS) in a wide-complex tachycardia strongly supports ventricular tachycardia. A regular wide-complex tachycardia should be treated as VT until proven otherwise; misreading it as SVT with aberrancy and giving an AV-nodal blocker can precipitate collapse.

In bradycardia, distinguish sinus bradycardia (fit athletes, sleep, beta-blocker effect, hypothyroidism, raised intracranial pressure) from AV block. For a future neurosurgeon, remember the Cushing reflex: hypertension, bradycardia and irregular breathing signal raised intracranial pressure and impending herniation. An ECG showing bradycardia in a head-injured patient is a neurological sign, not just a cardiac one.

**Axis.** A new right axis deviation in a breathless patient, especially with sinus tachycardia, a right bundle branch block or the S1Q3T3 pattern, raises the question of acute right ventricular strain such as pulmonary embolism. S1Q3T3 is specific but insensitive; sinus tachycardia is the most common ECG finding in PE. New left axis deviation may reflect left anterior fascicular block; combined with a right bundle branch block it forms a bifascicular block, which matters if the patient also has a long PR or syncope.

Always reconcile the tracing with the patient's pulse: pulseless electrical activity can show an organized rhythm on the monitor.

keyPoints: Normal resting rate 60-100 bpm; 300 ÷ large boxes between R waves for regular rhythms
For irregular rhythms, count QRS complexes on a 6- or 10-second strip and multiply
Normal sinus rhythm: P before every QRS, upright P in lead II, regular, 60-100 bpm
Normal axis −30° to +90°; lead I and aVF both positive = normal
I positive + aVF negative + II negative = left axis deviation; I negative + aVF positive = right axis deviation

test.q: There are 4 large boxes between consecutive R waves. What is the heart rate?
A heart rate of 48 bpm in an adult is called:
test.explain: Below 60 bpm is bradycardia. It can be normal in trained athletes.

test.q: The rhythm is irregularly irregular. Which method is best for the rate?
choices: Count QRS complexes in a 6-second strip × 10
test.explain: Box methods assume regular R-R intervals. In irregular rhythms, count complexes over a fixed time and multiply.

test.q: Which is NOT a criterion for normal sinus rhythm?
choices: Upright P waves in lead II
test.explain: A wide QRS is not part of the definition of sinus rhythm (and is abnormal). The other three are standard criteria.

test.q: Lead I positive and aVF positive means the axis is:
test.explain: Both positive places the axis between 0° and +90°, within the normal range.

test.q: Lead I negative and aVF positive means:
test.explain: A vector pointing away from lead I but toward aVF lies beyond +90°: right axis deviation.

test.q: Lead I positive, aVF negative and lead II positive. The axis is:
test.explain: If lead II is still positive, the axis has not passed −30°, so it is within normal limits.

test.q: Which is a classic cause of right axis deviation?
test.explain: RV hypertrophy shifts electrical forces rightward. The other options typically cause left axis deviation.

test.q: Heart rate rises on inspiration and falls on expiration in a healthy teenager. This is:
test.explain: Respiratory sinus arrhythmia is a normal autonomic variation, especially prominent in young people.

test.q: There are 2 large boxes between R waves, so the heart rate is ___ bpm.
test.explain: 300 ÷ 2 = 150. A regular narrow rate of 150 should prompt a look for atrial flutter with 2:1 block.

test.q: The normal QRS axis range is from −30° to ___ degrees.
test.explain: Normal axis is −30° to +90°. Beyond +90° is right axis deviation.

test.q: A rhythm with no pattern at all to its R-R intervals is described as irregularly ___.
test.explain: Irregularly irregular rhythm is the hallmark of atrial fibrillation.

test.q: Upper limit of normal adult resting heart rate (bpm)?
test.explain: Normal resting rate is 60-100 bpm; above 100 is tachycardia.

kidTest.q: What is the first question doctors ask about an ECG?
choices: How fast is the heart going?
kidTest.explain: Doctors first check how fast the heart is beating.

kidTest.q: A healthy heartbeat sounds like:
kidTest.explain: A healthy heart beats evenly, like a clock.

kidTest.q: If heartbeats are jumbled like popcorn, it means:
kidTest.explain: Jumbled beats can mean the heart's rhythm is off, so doctors look closer.

kidTest.q: Which way does the heart's electricity normally go?
kidTest.explain: Normally the spark slides down and to the left, like a playground slide.

kidTest.q: A heart that beats too slowly is called:
kidTest.explain: Brady means slow. Tachy means fast.

kidTest.q: What do doctors count to find how fast the heart beats: the big spikes or the paper?
kidTest.explain: Each big spike is one heartbeat, so counting them tells how fast the heart is going.

advancedTest.q: Lead I shows qR, aVF shows rS, lead II is predominantly negative, and the axis is about −60°. QRS is 100 ms. Best diagnosis?
advancedTest.explain: Marked left axis deviation (beyond −45°) with qR in I/aVL and rS inferiorly and a normal-width QRS is left anterior fascicular block.

advancedTest.q: A regular narrow-complex tachycardia at exactly 150 bpm with no clear P waves. What should you specifically look for?
choices: Flutter waves suggesting atrial flutter with 2:1 block
advancedTest.explain: Atrial flutter with an atrial rate near 300 and 2:1 conduction gives a ventricular rate near 150; flutter waves often hide in the QRS or T.

advancedTest.q: A head-injured patient develops hypertension, bradycardia and irregular respirations. The bradycardia most likely reflects:
choices: Cushing reflex from raised intracranial pressure
advancedTest.explain: The Cushing triad signals raised ICP and possible impending herniation: a neurosurgical emergency.

advancedTest.q: In the hexaxial system, which limb lead sits at +90°?
advancedTest.explain: aVF points straight down at +90°; lead I is 0°, II is +60°, III is +120°, aVL is −30°.

lessons.title: Common Arrhythmias

levels.kid:
An arrhythmia means the heart's beat has gotten mixed up.

Sometimes the top rooms of the heart just wiggle and shiver instead of squeezing. That's called atrial fibrillation. The heartbeat feels jumbled.

Sometimes the heart races super fast, like a drum solo that won't stop.

Sometimes the message from the top rooms gets stuck at the gate and doesn't reach the bottom rooms. That's called a heart block, and the heart can get too slow.

The scariest one is when the bottom rooms just shiver and don't pump at all. Then people need a shock from a special machine to restart the rhythm.
levels.hs:
An arrhythmia is any abnormal heart rhythm. The most important ones:
- **Atrial fibrillation (AF)**: chaotic electrical activity in the atria. No real P waves, and the rhythm is irregularly irregular. It is the most common sustained arrhythmia, especially in older people. The danger: blood can pool in the atria and form clots that travel to the brain, causing stroke.
- **Atrial flutter**: a fast, organized circuit in the right atrium making a sawtooth pattern of flutter waves.
- **Supraventricular tachycardia (SVT)**: a fast, regular, narrow-QRS rhythm, often from a short circuit near the AV node. Common in young, healthy people.
- **Ventricular tachycardia (VT)**: a fast rhythm from the ventricles with wide QRS complexes. It can drop blood pressure and turn into VF.
- **Ventricular fibrillation (VF)**: chaotic ventricular activity with no pumping. This is cardiac arrest. Treatment is CPR and defibrillation.
- **Heart blocks**: delayed or blocked signals through the AV node. First-degree is just a long PR interval. Second-degree means some beats are dropped. Third-degree (complete) block means the atria and ventricles beat independently, and the heart rate can be dangerously slow.

The key ECG questions: fast or slow, regular or irregular, narrow or wide QRS, and what are the P waves doing?
levels.college:
Classify arrhythmias by rate (brady vs tachy), QRS width (narrow = supraventricular, wide = ventricular or aberrant) and regularity.

**Narrow-complex tachycardias**
- Sinus tachycardia: normal P waves; a response to something (fever, pain, hypovolemia, anemia, pulmonary embolism). Treat the cause.
- Atrial fibrillation: irregularly irregular, no P waves, fibrillatory baseline. Management rests on rate or rhythm control plus stroke prevention with anticoagulation guided by a risk score (CHA2DS2-VASc).
- Atrial flutter: sawtooth flutter waves around 300 per minute, often with 2:1 conduction (ventricular rate about 150).
- AV nodal reentrant tachycardia (AVNRT) and AV reentrant tachycardia (AVRT, via an accessory pathway): regular, abrupt onset and offset. Vagal maneuvers or adenosine can terminate them by transiently blocking the AV node.

**Wide-complex tachycardias**
- Ventricular tachycardia: wide QRS, often with AV dissociation, fusion or capture beats. Unstable VT requires synchronized cardioversion; pulseless VT is treated like VF.
- Torsades de pointes: polymorphic VT with twisting QRS axis, associated with long QT. Magnesium is a mainstay of treatment.
- Ventricular fibrillation: chaotic, no pulse. Immediate defibrillation.

**Bradyarrhythmias and AV block**
- First-degree: PR over 200 ms, every P conducted.
- Second-degree Mobitz I (Wenckebach): PR progressively lengthens until a P is not conducted. Usually AV-nodal and benign.
- Second-degree Mobitz II: constant PR with sudden non-conducted P waves. Usually infranodal and can progress to complete block; pacing is often indicated.
- Third-degree: complete AV dissociation; the escape rhythm sets the rate (junctional narrow or ventricular wide).

**Pre-excitation (WPW)**: short PR, delta wave, wide QRS from an accessory pathway.
levels.phd:
Arrhythmias arise from three mechanisms: abnormal automaticity, triggered activity and reentry.

**Automaticity.** Pacemaker cells depolarize in phase 4 via the funny current (HCN channels) and calcium clock mechanisms. Enhanced or abnormal automaticity in ectopic foci, promoted by catecholamines, ischemia or hypokalemia, produces ectopic beats and some atrial and junctional tachycardias.

**Triggered activity.** Early afterdepolarizations occur during phases 2 to 3 when repolarization is prolonged (long QT, bradycardia, hypokalemia) and L-type calcium channels reactivate; they underlie torsades. Delayed afterdepolarizations occur after full repolarization when the sarcoplasmic reticulum is calcium-overloaded, driving the sodium-calcium exchanger inward; digoxin toxicity and catecholaminergic polymorphic VT (RyR2 mutations) are classic examples.

**Reentry.** Requires a circuit, unidirectional block and a conduction time longer than the refractory period of the tissue ahead (the wavelength concept: wavelength = conduction velocity × refractory period). Short wavelengths favor reentry. AVNRT uses dual AV-nodal pathways; AVRT uses an accessory pathway, orthodromic when antegrade down the node (narrow QRS) and antidromic when antegrade down the pathway (wide QRS). Typical atrial flutter is a macroreentrant circuit around the tricuspid annulus, through the cavotricuspid isthmus, which is why isthmus ablation is curative.

Atrial fibrillation is initiated mainly by ectopic triggers in the pulmonary vein sleeves and maintained by atrial remodeling: electrical remodeling shortens refractoriness ('AF begets AF') and structural remodeling (fibrosis, dilation) creates conduction heterogeneity. Pulmonary vein isolation by ablation targets the triggers.

Ventricular fibrillation is sustained by multiple wandering wavelets and rotors. Most sudden cardiac deaths in adults result from VF in the setting of ischemic or structural heart disease, while inherited channelopathies (long QT, Brugada, CPVT) explain a meaningful share in the young.
levels.expert:
At the bedside, the first question is not 'what rhythm is this?' but 'is the patient stable?' Instability means hypotension, shock, altered mental status, ischemic chest pain or acute heart failure. An unstable tachyarrhythmia gets electricity (synchronized cardioversion; unsynchronized defibrillation if pulseless VT or VF), not a long interpretive discussion.

Pearls that change management:
- **Wide and regular = VT until proven otherwise.** Older age and structural heart disease make VT far more likely than SVT with aberrancy. Clues: AV dissociation, capture or fusion beats, very wide QRS, extreme axis, concordance across the precordial leads.
- **Irregular, wide and very fast** (rates well above 200) in a young patient suggests AF with WPW pre-excitation. Avoid AV-nodal blockers (adenosine, calcium-channel blockers, beta-blockers, digoxin) because they can favor conduction down the accessory pathway and precipitate VF; cardioversion or a pathway-slowing agent is used instead.
- **Adenosine is diagnostic as well as therapeutic.** Transient AV block terminates reentry through the node or unmasks flutter waves or atrial tachycardia. Warn the patient about a brief sense of doom; record a strip while giving it.
- **AF and stroke.** Anticoagulation decisions follow stroke risk (CHA2DS2-VASc) weighed against bleeding risk, not whether rhythm control has 'cured' the AF. AF is a major cause of cardioembolic stroke, including large-vessel occlusions that neuro-interventionalists treat with thrombectomy.
- **Mobitz II and complete heart block** in a symptomatic patient need pacing readiness: transcutaneous pacing pads on, and plan for transvenous or permanent pacing. Atropine works on the AV node and is unreliable for infranodal block.
- **Look for the reversible cause**: hyperkalemia, ischemia, drug toxicity (digoxin, beta-blockers, calcium-channel blockers), hypothyroidism, raised intracranial pressure, hypoxia.

keyPoints: AF: irregularly irregular, no P waves; major cause of cardioembolic stroke
Atrial flutter: sawtooth waves ~300/min, often 2:1 block giving a rate ~150
SVT: narrow, regular, abrupt; vagal maneuvers or adenosine can stop AV-nodal reentry
Wide regular tachycardia = treat as VT until proven otherwise; VF = defibrillate
AV block: 1st = long PR; Mobitz I = progressive PR then drop; Mobitz II = sudden drop; 3rd = AV dissociation

test.q: An irregularly irregular rhythm with no visible P waves is most likely:
test.explain: AF has chaotic atrial activity (no organized P waves) and irregular ventricular response. Flutter is usually regular with sawtooth waves.

test.q: The most feared complication of atrial fibrillation is:
test.explain: Stasis in the fibrillating left atrium, especially the appendage, allows clots that can embolize to the brain.

test.q: A sawtooth baseline in leads II, III and aVF suggests:
test.explain: Typical flutter produces negative sawtooth flutter waves in the inferior leads.

test.q: PR interval progressively lengthens until a P wave is not followed by a QRS. This is:
test.explain: Progressive PR prolongation then a dropped beat defines Wenckebach, usually an AV-nodal and benign block.

test.q: PR is constant, but occasionally a P wave is suddenly not conducted. This is:
test.explain: Mobitz II has a fixed PR with sudden dropped beats; it is usually below the AV node and can progress to complete block.

test.q: P waves and QRS complexes march at their own unrelated rates. This is:
test.explain: Complete AV dissociation, with an escape rhythm driving the ventricles, defines third-degree block.

test.q: What is the immediate treatment for ventricular fibrillation?
test.explain: VF produces no cardiac output. CPR and defibrillation as fast as possible are what save lives.

test.q: A regular wide-complex tachycardia in a 70-year-old with a prior heart attack should be treated as:
test.explain: Structural heart disease makes VT far more likely, and treating VT as SVT can be dangerous.

test.q: Which arrhythmia is classically associated with a long QT interval?
test.explain: Long QT enables early afterdepolarizations that trigger torsades, a polymorphic VT with twisting QRS.

test.q: Short PR interval plus a delta wave indicates:
test.explain: An accessory pathway bypasses the AV node, giving a short PR and slurred QRS upstroke (delta wave).

test.q: In atrial flutter with 2:1 block, the ventricular rate is often about ___ bpm.
test.explain: Atrial rate ~300 with every second wave conducted gives ~150.

test.q: Which drug, given rapidly, briefly blocks the AV node and can stop AV-nodal reentrant SVT?
test.explain: Adenosine causes transient AV-nodal block, terminating reentry through the node.

test.q: Name the arrhythmia: chaotic, pulseless, no identifiable QRS complexes.
test.explain: Ventricular fibrillation is cardiac arrest; defibrillate immediately.

kidTest.q: What does arrhythmia mean?
kidTest.explain: An arrhythmia means the heartbeat isn't keeping its normal steady rhythm.

kidTest.q: In atrial fibrillation, the top rooms of the heart:
kidTest.explain: The top rooms quiver instead of squeezing in an organized way.

kidTest.q: A heart block means the message gets stuck at:
choices: The gate between top and bottom rooms
kidTest.explain: The AV node is the gate. If the message is stuck there, the bottom rooms may beat too slowly.

kidTest.q: If the bottom rooms only shiver and don't pump, people need:
choices: A shock from a special machine
kidTest.explain: A defibrillator gives a shock that can restart a normal rhythm, along with CPR.

kidTest.q: SVT makes the heart go:
kidTest.explain: SVT is a fast, racing heartbeat.

kidTest.q: What do we call a heartbeat that is mixed up? (starts with 'a')
kidTest.explain: Arrhythmia means an abnormal heart rhythm.

advancedTest.q: A young patient has an irregular, very fast (around 250 bpm) wide-complex tachycardia with varying QRS shapes. Which drug class should be avoided?
choices: AV-nodal blockers such as adenosine or calcium-channel blockers
advancedTest.explain: This suggests AF with WPW pre-excitation. Blocking the AV node can increase conduction down the accessory pathway and degenerate into VF.

advancedTest.q: Why does cavotricuspid isthmus ablation cure typical atrial flutter?
choices: The flutter is a macroreentrant circuit around the tricuspid annulus that must pass through the isthmus
advancedTest.explain: Typical flutter circulates around the tricuspid annulus; a line of block across the isthmus breaks the circuit.

advancedTest.q: Digoxin toxicity causes arrhythmias mainly through:
choices: Delayed afterdepolarizations from intracellular calcium overload
Loss of SA node automaticity only
advancedTest.explain: Na/K-ATPase inhibition raises intracellular calcium; SR calcium overload causes delayed afterdepolarizations (triggered activity).

advancedTest.q: In complete heart block with a wide escape rhythm and hypotension, why is atropine often ineffective?
choices: Atropine only works in the lungs
The block is usually infranodal, below where vagal tone acts
advancedTest.explain: Atropine reduces vagal effect on the SA and AV nodes; a wide escape suggests block below the node, so pacing is needed.

lessons.title: Ischemia and Infarction on the ECG

levels.kid:
Heart muscle needs blood, just like you need food. Blood comes through little tubes called coronary arteries.

If one of those tubes gets blocked, part of the heart muscle gets hungry and starts to hurt. That is a heart attack.

The ECG can show this! A flat part of the line that should sit on the ground gets lifted up, like a tent. Doctors call it ST elevation.

When they see it, they hurry, because the blocked tube needs to be opened fast. Every minute counts, so the heart muscle can be saved.
levels.hs:
Myocardial ischemia means heart muscle is not getting enough oxygen, usually because a coronary artery is narrowed or blocked by plaque and a clot. If the blockage lasts, the muscle dies: a myocardial infarction (MI), or heart attack.

The ECG changes to know:
- **ST elevation**: the ST segment rises above the baseline. When it appears in two or more neighboring leads, it suggests a full-thickness injury from a completely blocked artery: an ST-elevation MI (STEMI). This is an emergency; the artery needs to be opened quickly, usually with a catheter and stent.
- **ST depression and T-wave inversion**: suggest ischemia that is not full thickness, seen in some heart attacks without ST elevation (NSTEMI) and in unstable angina.
- **Pathologic Q waves**: deep, wide Q waves that can appear after muscle has died and may remain forever as a scar marker.

Leads tell you where the problem is:
- Inferior wall: II, III, aVF (usually right coronary artery).
- Anterior wall: V1 to V4 (left anterior descending artery).
- Lateral wall: I, aVL, V5, V6 (circumflex artery or branches).

A normal ECG does not rule out a heart attack. Doctors also check a blood test for troponin, a protein released from damaged heart muscle, and repeat the ECG.
levels.college:
Acute coronary syndrome (ACS) spans unstable angina, NSTEMI and STEMI. The ECG triages the patient: STEMI needs immediate reperfusion, ideally primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) within a short door-to-balloon time, or fibrinolysis if PCI is unavailable in time.

**STEMI criteria** (in the absence of LBBB or LVH): new ST elevation at the J point in at least two contiguous leads, at least 1 mm in most leads. Leads V2 and V3 require higher thresholds: at least 2 mm in men 40 or older, 2.5 mm in men under 40, and 1.5 mm in women.

**Territories**
- Septal V1 to V2, anterior V3 to V4: left anterior descending (LAD).
- Lateral I, aVL, V5 to V6: left circumflex or diagonal branches.
- Inferior II, III, aVF: right coronary artery in most people (right-dominant), circumflex in others.
- Posterior: ST depression with tall R waves in V1 to V3, the mirror image of a posterior STEMI; confirm with posterior leads V7 to V9.
- Right ventricle: ST elevation in right-sided lead V4R, accompanying an inferior MI.

**Reciprocal changes**, ST depression in leads opposite the injured wall (for example aVL in inferior STEMI), increase confidence that ST elevation is from infarction rather than a mimic.

**Evolution**: hyperacute T waves (minutes) → ST elevation (minutes to hours) → Q waves (hours to days) → T-wave inversion → ST normalization. Persistent ST elevation weeks later suggests a ventricular aneurysm.

**Mimics of ST elevation**: pericarditis (diffuse concave ST elevation, PR depression, no reciprocal changes except aVR), early repolarization, LBBB, LVH, Brugada pattern and hyperkalemia.

Troponin defines infarction (a rise and/or fall with at least one value above the 99th percentile, plus clinical evidence of ischemia), but the decision to reperfuse STEMI is made from the ECG, not by waiting for troponin.
levels.phd:
ECG changes in ischemia arise from the electrophysiology of injured myocardium. Ischemic cells lose ATP-dependent ion pumping; extracellular potassium accumulates, the resting membrane potential becomes less negative, and action potential amplitude and duration fall. Opening of ATP-sensitive potassium channels further shortens the action potential.

The resulting voltage gradients between injured and healthy tissue produce injury currents. In transmural ischemia, the injured zone faces the overlying electrode. During diastole the injured tissue is partially depolarized, producing a diastolic current that depresses the TQ baseline; during systole the healthy tissue is fully depolarized while the injured tissue is less so, producing a systolic injury current toward the electrode. Because ECG machines use AC coupling and display the TQ segment as baseline, both effects appear as ST elevation. In subendocardial ischemia the injury vector points toward the ventricular cavity, away from surface electrodes, producing ST depression that does not localize the culprit artery.

Pathologic Q waves reflect an electrically silent region: the electrode looks through a 'window' of dead tissue and records the cavity potential, a negative deflection.

The binary STEMI/NSTEMI model has well-known limitations. Studies of patients with NSTEMI find that roughly a quarter have an acutely occluded culprit artery, often the circumflex, whose territory is electrically under-represented on the standard 12 leads. This motivated the occlusion MI (OMI) paradigm, which recognizes subtle or non-criteria patterns of acute coronary occlusion: de Winter T waves (upsloping ST depression with tall symmetric T waves in the precordial leads, suggesting proximal LAD occlusion), hyperacute T waves, posterior MI, and subtle reciprocal ST depression in aVL heralding inferior occlusion. Wellens syndrome (deep or biphasic T inversion in V2 to V3 in a pain-free patient) marks critical proximal LAD stenosis after reperfusion.

For LBBB and ventricular pacing, the Sgarbossa criteria and their modified Smith version use concordant ST deviation and an excessive ST/S ratio to detect occlusion despite abnormal baseline repolarization.
levels.expert:
With chest pain, the ECG should be obtained and read within minutes of arrival. Senior clinicians follow a few habits.

- **Compare and repeat.** A single normal ECG does not exclude ACS. Repeat it every 15 to 30 minutes while symptoms persist and whenever pain changes. Dynamic change is the signal; an old ECG tells you what is new.
- **Look at aVL in every inferior read.** Subtle ST depression or T inversion in aVL can be the earliest sign of inferior occlusion.
- **Think posterior.** ST depression maximal in V1 to V3 in a patient with ongoing pain may be a posterior STEMI, not an NSTEMI. Record V7 to V9 and treat as occlusion if confirmed.
- **Right ventricular infarction.** In inferior STEMI, record V4R. RV infarction makes the patient preload-dependent: nitrates and aggressive diuresis can cause profound hypotension, and fluids are often needed.
- **aVR elevation with widespread ST depression** suggests diffuse subendocardial ischemia from left main or multivessel disease, or a supply-demand mismatch (severe anemia, hypotension, tachyarrhythmia). It is a high-risk pattern needing urgent discussion with cardiology.
- **Do not let criteria override the patient.** Persistent ischemic pain despite treatment with a non-diagnostic ECG is an indication for urgent angiography in guideline frameworks.

Neurology overlaps: severe brain injury, especially subarachnoid hemorrhage, can produce deep symmetrical T-wave inversions ('cerebral T waves'), QT prolongation and even troponin rise from catecholamine-mediated myocardial stunning (including takotsubo-like patterns). Before sending a comatose patient with abnormal ECG to the cath lab, think about the head CT. Conversely, stroke patients need ECG monitoring to detect atrial fibrillation as the embolic source.

Finally, ECG and troponin are partners: ECG for reperfusion decisions now, serial high-sensitivity troponin for diagnosis over hours.

keyPoints: ST elevation in ≥2 contiguous leads (with lead-specific thresholds) suggests STEMI: reperfuse fast
Inferior II, III, aVF (usually RCA); anterior V1-V4 (LAD); lateral I, aVL, V5-V6 (circumflex)
Reciprocal ST depression supports a true STEMI; pericarditis shows diffuse ST elevation with PR depression
Posterior MI shows ST depression and tall R in V1-V3; confirm with V7-V9
A normal ECG doesn't rule out ACS: repeat ECGs and serial troponin

test.q: ST elevation in leads II, III and aVF indicates injury to which wall?
test.explain: II, III and aVF view the inferior wall, usually supplied by the right coronary artery.

test.q: ST elevation in V1 to V4 most likely involves which artery?
test.explain: The anterior and septal leads look at territory supplied by the LAD.

test.q: Which blood test marker indicates heart muscle damage?
test.explain: Troponin is released by injured cardiac myocytes and is the standard biomarker for MI.

test.q: Which finding supports true STEMI rather than a mimic?
choices: Reciprocal ST depression in opposite leads
Diffuse ST elevation in nearly all leads
test.explain: Reciprocal changes point to localized transmural injury. Diffuse ST elevation with PR depression suggests pericarditis.

test.q: A patient has diffuse concave ST elevation and PR depression after a viral illness, with pain worse lying flat. Most likely:
test.explain: Pericarditis classically causes widespread ST elevation, PR depression and positional pleuritic pain.

test.q: What do pathologic Q waves usually indicate?
test.explain: Q waves reflect an electrically silent area of necrosis or scar.

test.q: ST depression with tall R waves in V1 to V3 in a patient with ongoing chest pain may be:
test.explain: This is the mirror image of posterior ST elevation; posterior leads V7 to V9 confirm it.

test.q: A single normal ECG in someone with ongoing chest pain:
choices: Does not rule out ACS; repeat ECG and check troponin
Means the pain is from the lungs
test.explain: Early ECGs can be normal or subtle. Serial ECGs and troponin are needed.

test.q: Which is the preferred reperfusion therapy for STEMI when available quickly?
test.explain: Opening the artery with a catheter and stent (primary PCI) is preferred when it can be done promptly.

test.q: In inferior STEMI with right ventricular involvement, which treatment can cause dangerous hypotension?
test.explain: RV infarction is preload-dependent; nitrates reduce preload and can crash blood pressure.

test.q: Leads I, aVL, V5 and V6 look at the ___ wall of the left ventricle.
test.explain: These are the lateral leads, typically the circumflex or diagonal territory.

test.q: What does STEMI stand for?
test.explain: STEMI = ST-elevation myocardial infarction, a full-thickness infarct needing urgent reperfusion.

test.q: Which right-sided lead is recorded to look for right ventricular infarction?
test.explain: V4R, placed at the right midclavicular line in the fifth intercostal space, detects RV involvement.

kidTest.q: What do coronary arteries do?
choices: Bring blood to the heart muscle
kidTest.explain: Coronary arteries are the heart's own blood tubes.

kidTest.q: A heart attack happens when:
kidTest.explain: When a coronary artery is blocked, part of the heart muscle gets hungry for blood and is hurt.

kidTest.q: On the ECG, a heart attack can lift the line up like a:
kidTest.explain: ST elevation looks like the line got lifted up like a tent.

kidTest.q: Why do doctors hurry for a heart attack?
choices: Every minute of blockage hurts more heart muscle
kidTest.explain: Opening the tube quickly saves heart muscle.

kidTest.q: What do heart muscles need from blood?
kidTest.explain: Blood brings oxygen that the heart muscle needs to work.

kidTest.q: What is it called when a heart tube is blocked and heart muscle gets hurt? (two words: heart ___)
kidTest.explain: A heart attack is when blocked blood flow damages heart muscle.

advancedTest.q: Why does transmural ischemia appear as ST elevation on the surface ECG?
choices: Q waves push the ST segment up
The atria repolarize during the ST segment
Injury currents from partially depolarized tissue shift the TQ baseline and ST segment toward the overlying electrode
advancedTest.explain: Diastolic injury current depresses the TQ baseline and systolic injury current raises ST; with TQ displayed as baseline, both read as ST elevation.

advancedTest.q: Upsloping ST depression with tall, symmetric precordial T waves in a patient with acute chest pain suggests:
choices: De Winter pattern: proximal LAD occlusion
advancedTest.explain: De Winter T waves are an OMI pattern equivalent to anterior STEMI.

advancedTest.q: A pain-free patient after recent chest pain has deep, symmetric T inversions in V2 to V3 and normal ST segments. This is:
choices: Wellens syndrome, warning of critical proximal LAD stenosis
advancedTest.explain: Wellens marks reperfused but critically stenosed LAD; stress testing can be dangerous and angiography is indicated.

advancedTest.q: A comatose patient with sudden severe headache has deep symmetric T inversions, long QT and mildly raised troponin. What should be considered before coronary angiography?
choices: Subarachnoid hemorrhage with neurogenic cardiac changes
advancedTest.explain: SAH can cause cerebral T waves and catecholamine-mediated myocardial stunning; head CT changes management completely.
